## The tree

`Ui_DrawScreen` (0x00475A50) is the definition table's `+32` callback for **34 of the 37 screens**, so it's the generic renderer, and walking it settles the structure:

```
screen   124 B, three slots            flags +112/+116
  panel  one drawn (+28), one leaving (+32)   +72/+76
    list up to ten, at panel+32              +16/+20
      item 72 B                        +48/+52/+56
```

That also answers a loose end from the primitives pass: there are four flag-helper pairs because there are four levels, each with its own flag words. The bank in a constant picks the word, so the same constant means different things at different levels. Full field map now in `readable/types.h`.

## What it draws

**An item is a bag of bits, not a type.** `Ui_DrawItem` draws the text, then tests one flag per decoration — fill, outline, cursor, four scroll arrows, the ▶ marker, a lit/unlit sprite — each its own primitive. The arrows guard `0x403C0000` is **exactly the OR** of the four bits the arrow drawer then tests one at a time, which is the kind of agreement that says the bit assignment is read rather than fitted.

**The background is a tile map.** `panel+20` is 80 tile ids over a 10×8 grid of 64×64 cells, each id selecting source cell `(id%10, id/10)`. The arithmetic checks itself: 10×64 = 640, seven rows of 64 leave exactly the 32 that the code hard-codes as a half row (source y 448..480), and **all 11 shipped bitmaps are 640×480**. That's how `boutiq.bmp` serves ten shops and `gfxint.bmp` all the menus — one sheet, a different 80-byte map.

**Panels slide, items mostly don't.** One start/delta/duration/elapsed set on the panel; `Ui_ItemScreenX/Y` add the current offset to every item.

Two things that explain how the menus actually look:
- an unselected row is dimmed by `>>= 1` on all three colour channels — one shift, and it's every dim row in the game;
- **`item+36` is a font id, not a character.** It becomes `Text_DrawBlock`'s `params[2]`, whose default is the same **74** the rows carry (76 below 640×480). So last session's "style byte 83/74" is settled: `Opt_BindRow` picking 83 for a heading is picking a typeface. Read as ASCII they're 'S' and 'J' — an inviting coincidence, now named as one.

## One place the decompiler is wrong

`Ui_Oscillator`: Hex-Rays renders the base as `4996768` (0x004C3EE0); the asm's `lea eax,[eax+eax*4]` / `lea eax, ds:4C3EA0h[eax*8]` is `0x004C3EA0 + 40*k`. Taking the C would have put every record **24 bytes out**. Read correctly it's 8 timers ending exactly where the string block begins — and **number 2 runs 45..200 over a second**, the alpha every arrow, marker and pulsing fill throbs with. I asserted the base in `verify.py` since that's the part a re-derivation would get wrong.

## The chain, end to end

`Text_DrawBlock` was already CLEAN but only unpacks parameters. The work is `Text_LayOutBlock` (markup, word wrap, styled runs) and `Text_DrawRun` (rasterise one run).

A **13-record font table** at 0x004C7090 keys each face by an ASCII **letter**, and all 13 names ship in `fr/FONTS` — exactly 13 there, no spares. That's what `item+36` has been all along:

- **74 is `J`, JOURNAL** — the engine's own default and every option row
- **83 is `S`, SNEAK** — what `Opt_BindRow` gives a heading, and it *is* two pixels taller (line 20 vs 17)
- **76 is `L`, SMALL** — the sub-640×480 override, and it really is smaller (12 vs 17)

So the "83/74 style byte" thread that started two sessions ago closes properly: they're typefaces, and the sizes confirm the roles.

## The `.FNT` format

256 8-byte glyph records, then pixels from byte 2048 — the record's `+0` being an offset in **eight-byte units** is the part that had to be right. **2899 glyph blocks, 0 landing outside their file, 0 overlapping**, data starting at exactly 2048 in all 13, and every font covering exactly codes 33..255 (space deliberately absent, so it falls to the default advance). And it draws: `tools/fnt.py journal A g É ?` prints recognisable accented letters.

**A pixel byte is a coverage level 0..31, not a colour** — `Text_DrawRun` rebuilds a 32-entry ramp of the requested colour (IDA itself types it `__int16[32]`), so the fonts are greyscale antialiasing coloured at draw time.

## Two things worth flagging

**A shipped defect.** 485 875 of 485 877 pixel bytes are in 0..31. The two that aren't are both in SMALL's `!` — 125 and 133, indexing ~200 bytes past the ramp into whatever globals follow. Asserted at *exactly* 2 so it stays a known quantity rather than drifting into "close enough".

**A docs correction.** `FILE_FORMATS.md` §5b4 recorded the markup as "`{C}`/`{fC}` centering, `{I RRGGBB}` color triplets". `{fC}` is the **COMPUTER font**, not centring, and the colour is **nine decimal digits** `RRRGGGBBB`. The shipped text confirms the decode from the other side: **329 `{f<letter>}` directives and every operand is one of the 13 ids that exist**, plus 111 well-formed `{I255120045}`-style colours. Both docs now say so.

Also decoded: directives **chain inside one brace** (`{fCC}` = font C then command C), and an *unrecognised* letter falls through to the line flush — which is how `{P}` works as a paragraph break without being implemented at all.

Two of my own selftest assertions failed on first run (I'd guessed the id letter was always the name's initial, and invented a line-height relationship). Both were wrong; I replaced them with measured invariants.

## There are no per-screen input handlers

The 37-record screen table's `+24` — the input callback — is **`0x0042A0F0` for all 32 live screens**; the five `(ELIMINE)` entries are null and nothing else varies. The slot distribution:

| slot | distinct |
|---|---|
| `+20` open | **21** |
| `+24` input | **1** |
| `+28` close | **11** |
| `+32` draw | 2 |

So the per-screen work lives in **open** and **close**, not input. That note came from me two sessions ago (`RECONSTRUCTION` said "the per-screen input handlers, 0x004AExxx–0x004B0xxx, one family per screen kind") — it's now corrected, and `verify.py: ui input` asserts the whole distribution so it can't drift back.

## What the shared handler actually does

**The bits are the game's, not the menu's.** `Game_Frame` polls once and edge-filters against a repeat mask; `Ui_BeginScreen` sets that mask to **0x203F** — every button the interface uses — which is why holding a direction doesn't scroll a menu. The word is the engine's **14 key-binding slots**, the same one `.CTL` transitions match on (already documented in `ASSETS` from the combat side; my read of `0x004C65B8` agrees with it independently). The interface just gives three bits a second job:

- **0x10 confirm** (E), **0x20 back** (R), **0x2000 close** (TAB)

and the joystick's first ten buttons land on `0x10` upward, so pad button 0 is confirm and button 1 is back — matching E and R.

**Dispatch** delegates in a fixed order: panel's hook `+16` → the *current* list's hook `+4` → `Ui_MoveSelection`. That default steps the selection **over every `UIF_UNSELECTABLE` item**, so a caption or disabled row is skipped rather than landed on, and when no direction was pressed it falls straight through to confirm — which is why one function serves both.

## The unification worth having

`Ui_ConfirmSelection` takes the item's `+40` callback if it has one, and otherwise **enters the panel at `+44`**: old panel's leave hook, rethread the screen's `+28/+32/+36`, call the new panel's builder at `+4`.

That is exactly the options **page** record read as parent/builder/leave, and exactly the `+44` that `Opt_BindRow` writes for a submenu row. **The options page tree and the interface panel tree are one structure**, and this is the code that walks it. One variant: an item whose `+44` also carries `0x20000040` is entered *on the move* rather than the confirm — a tab strip.

Also read: `Input_ReadOneControl`'s single code space (keyboard scan 0..255, joystick button index + 48, mouse 12/13/14), which means a **type-3 option row's `+92` array is three device bindings, not the choice values it holds for every other type**.

## The obstacle was the decompilation, not the code

**26 of the 30 open/close addresses have no function in `Runtime.exe.c` — and no `proc` label in the listing either.** They carry no `push` prologue, so IDA folded each into whatever precedes it. That means `tools/asmfn.py`, which anchors on `loc_`/`proc` labels, **silently returns a different function** for most of them: four of my first six reads came back as the same unrelated block before I checked. That's the opcode-120 trap from `CLAUDE.md` §1, one address range further on, and it's now recorded there with the measured size of the gap asserted in `verify.py`.

I disassembled from the image instead (capstone in a scratch venv; the names live in `tools/ui_tables.py: CALLBACKS` since `readable/src` has nowhere to put them).

## The family is uniform, and that's the check

- **20 of 20 opens** write the screen's `+28` with a static panel address and reach `Ui_BeginScreen`
- **19 of 20 closes** are, or reach, `Ui_CloseScreenDefault`

Between those two lines each open only does bookkeeping. Seven screens share a *single* panel (`0x004E4108` — `TERMINAL`, `FIGHT SIM`, `MORGUE`, `ARCHIVES`, the three `SURV`), which is §2's `+8`-parameter story seen from the code side. `TERMINAL` is the clearest: its open writes five items' string ids **5–9** and tags **0–4**, plus a sixth with **10** — in `IAM\Term` those are "Consulter le dossier n°1…5" and "Quitter le terminal", with the dossier texts in strings 0–4.

## The shops name themselves

`Ui_OpenShop` switches on the fixed parameter through a jump table at `0x004AE7AC`, ten targets each one `mov word ptr [0x004E37CC], imm16` — the title in `IAM\Buy`. **Eight of the ten titles name the screen that uses them**: BANK→"Banque", PHARMACIE→"Pharmacie", ARMURERIE, SORCELLERIE, LIBRAIRIE, SEX-SHOP, DIVERS, LIB. LAHOREY→"Bibliothèque de Lahoreh". Shift the index by one and all eight break at once — a **third independent confirmation of the screen-table order**, and the strongest yet, since it's the engine mapping a parameter to a French title. RESTAURANT and BAR share the generic "Achat"; **BANK alone says *vente*** and takes the one branch the other nine skip.

## Two smaller closures

- **The one close in the game that can refuse.** `Ui_CloseSneakFamily` starts oscillator 5 at 100 ms *instead* of closing, and while its flag bit is set the close is declined — the sneak interface has a shutting animation. Every other screen closes on the frame it's told to.
- **Where `ui.open` comes back.** `Ui_CloseScreenDefault`'s tail, when the *last* screen closes, clears the input word (so the release of the closing button can't leak into the game) and calls `sub_466B60` — the function that fills the event-5 block with the waiting context and the answer. The suspend-at-status-6 loop in `SCRIPT_VM` §70 now has both ends.

## The data channel

The interface never touches an object list — it raises an event and reads back one argument block: `+0` the value in and out, `+4` the **result code** (1 done, 2 refused, 3 no list / past the end) and, for case 36, the *request* code on the way **in**, `+8` a text buffer.

| case | |
|---|---|
| 25/26 | open/close; opening list **3** also sizes it to 16 and loads it — list 3 is a shop's stock, per area |
| 29, 33, 34 | count; name **plus `" - N"`** when flag `0x20` says the item carries a quantity — from the **player** record for kinds 2..6, from the item's own `+12` for 7..11; price |
| 30 | the **3D preview** — skipped for list 2, which has no models |
| 35 | **use**: flag bit 1 = consumable (`Object_ApplyEffect`); otherwise load the model and hand back a slot — "use" on anything else means **drop it into the world** |
| 36, 38, 39 | move between lists 0 and 1; **buy** against the player's money at `+172`; **sell at half price**, clamped |
| 40, 41, 42 | examine; the shop's "you already have one" refusal; the script layer's veto |

A list slot is **56 bytes** — `char[32]` name then the `IAM\OBJECT` record's first 24 — so the fields these read are object-record fields: `+0` id, `+2` kind, `+4` flags, `+10` price, `+12` count, `+14` model stem.

## The combination table, and six recipes that cannot fire

Case 37 walks a table at **`GLOBAL +12`** (count `+26`): **11 records** of `[a][b][product][gate]`, matched **symmetrically** — order doesn't matter. All 33 ids name a real object and read as recipes: box + key → open box, explosive + detonator → charge, koil + sleeping pill → drugged koil, plus six spell recipes.

A recipe fires only when its `+6` **equals** `dword_4E6C70` — and that global has exactly **four references in the whole binary**, all inside this case: 1 when the first item picked is `GLOBAL +64` (object 330, *"Beshe'm sanctifié"*), 0 otherwise, −1 after a combine. **It is never 8.** I checked that in the assembly rather than the decompiler, since a surprising negative earns it.

So the six gate-8 spell recipes are dead, and nothing else grants their products: **0 of 472** world-script and **0 of 10** conversation-script `inventory.add` sites name any of the eleven.

**Checking the prop catalogue is what stopped me overstating it.** "Sort de résurrection" is placed **once as a world prop**, so it's reachable after all; the other five spell items — "Sort de vérité" in its four variants and "Sort démasquer un démon" — are unobtainable in the shipped build. Sixteen of the eighteen *ingredients* are placed as props, so it's the combination that's dead, not the ingredients. Same shape as the dead options page and the five `(ELIMINE)` screens.

## The fight AI was a `.CTL` section with a walk but no meaning

`.CTL` `+76`/`+80` sat in the header map with its contents blank — `anim_ctl.py` walked past it because the walk has to land exactly. It's the **fight AI**: 156-byte profiles keyed by `+0` = difficulty level + 1, with two delay ranges and **twelve situation slots** of moves. Slot 7 is the one `Fight_TickAI` reads at `+100`/`+104`, which fixes the stride and field order.

**The AI doesn't drive the actor — it presses buttons.** It hands a whole move to `Perso_InjectInput`, which loads it into the actor's input queue, so the AI and the player go through one state machine and a move reads as a combo: `E, idle, R, idle, F`. That's why the shipped lists are legible as fighting-game inputs.

**Three of the seven `.CTL` files carry profiles — exactly the three combat files.** Eleven profiles, and the **delay ladder is identical across files** (500–1000, 250–750, **100–200**, **3000–5000** ms) while the move counts differ — so a harder opponent is mostly a *shorter wait*, not a better move. Id 4 has one attack and four walk directions: a sparring partner, present only in the two Kay'l/female files.

All 30 distinct input words are real bindings, and their **union is `0xCFF`** — the AI presses ten of the fourteen and never CTRL, SPACE, SHIFT or TAB, the four non-combat ones.

Also pinned, because it's a confusable pair: `0x40000000` is the **queue's idle word** (`Perso_SetInputEnabled` resets to exactly it), *not* the `0x80000000` "no input" edge code. `Cef_InputMatches` ends `a1 == 0x80000000 ? a2 <= 0x2000`, so the idle word matches no idle edge — which is what puts a real gap between two presses.

## The shoot AI is four functions and no data

Total contrast. `Shoot_ActorEnter` reads the actor's **character type** (property 7) and installs one callback: type 7 `X-Tech` → `nullsub_9`, i.e. **nothing**; 10 `Gandhar` and 13 `Astaroth` get their own routines; everyone else shares one. `Shoot_Think` is the navigation half. No table — exactly what the plan meant by "thin, data-poor".

## Two things I did *not* claim

- **Which profile the shipped scripts select.** `Fight_Engage`'s second argument gives the level; two of three call sites pass a literal 1, the third is inside opcode **62 `fight.begin`**, whose operand length the VM table gives as 4 and `vm_oplen.py` reads from the handler as **6**. Decoding its fields under a disputed length would decide it and could as easily be wrong, so it's left open. (Separately: `Difficulté des combats` does *not* pick the profile — it sets `word_90E1A6`, a flat +0.5/+0.25/+0 bonus on one player stat.)
- I nearly enshrined a **case-sensitive glob** that found 5 `.CTL` files instead of 7 and missed two of the three profile sets. `anim_ctl.py`'s own listing caught it. The check now globs both cases and says why.

| bit | Aventure | Tirer | Combat |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x0010 | Action / Utiliser RET | Tir RSHIFT / **left mouse** | **Coup de poing 1 Q** |
| 0x0020 | Annuler / Sauter SPACE | Sauter SPACE / right mouse | **Coup de poing 2 W** |

I was wrong to blame the restarts. It was a real bug, and a nasty one.

## A backtick in a comment

Inside `/cutscene`'s GLSL vertex shader, a prose comment wrote the shimmer formula in markdown backticks:

```
 * The phase is `(clock >> 2) + (vertexAddress >> 4)`, and since the
```

The shader source is a **template literal**. The first of those backticks *closed it*, and what followed parsed as a tagged call on the resulting string — `` `…`(clock >> 2) `` — which is perfectly valid JavaScript. So `node --check` passed.

At run time it threw `ReferenceError: clock is not defined` inside `initGL` — and `boot()` calls `initGL()` **before** it fetches the catalogue. Hence: empty list, no visible symptom, everything server-side testing fine.

**A backtick in a comment inside a template literal is not a comment.**

## How I found it

## The fonts

`tools/uitext.py` follows `Text_LayOutBlock` and `Text_DrawRun` rather than approximating them: the shipped `.FNT` glyphs, the same 120%-of-line-height spacing, and a glyph pixel taken as a **coverage level 0..31** that becomes the alpha — which is exactly what lets one glyph sheet serve every colour.

## The markup

Every case the shipped text actually uses:

| | |
|---|---|
| `{fC}` | names a font by its id letter — COMPUTER here |
| `{I255120045}` | the colour, **three 3-digit decimals** (255,120,45), not a hex triple |
| `{fCI255120045}` | both chained inside one brace |
| `{C}` `{D}` `{G}` `{F}` | the four alignments — `{C}` centres |
| `{X030040}` | a move, in screen percentages |
| CR / LF | CR skipped, LF ends a line |

Font changes work mid-string: one terminal dossier parses as 647 characters of COMPUTER with **20 of SNEAK** inside it — that's `{fS}Anekbah{fC}` — and `IAM\Lift`'s two-line floor labels now render two lines tall because of the CRLF.

You can try it outside the browser too:

```

python3 tools/uitext.py --png out.png --font J "Nouvelle partie"
```

One thing I did *not* do: `{B}` blink and the `[...]` counted spans are parsed and skipped rather than rendered — blink needs oscillator 1 ticking, and a span's alternate style comes from the item's `+30`, which only matters where a row shows a label and a value together. They're logged as ignored rather than silently dropped.

## Why the viewer had them left

The four buttons store bank C as **zero**, which reads as `Text_DrawBlock`'s default alignment — left, against the edge of a 640-wide row. So reading the item record said "left", and that's what I drew.

But the record isn't the whole state. `Ui_OpenStartMenu` centres them with one line:

```
I2D_SetFlagOnAllRows(0x004CE820, 0x80000010, 1)
```

A **broadcast over every item of list 0** — and `Ui_ItemTextStyle` turns bank-C bit `0x10` into `TEXTP_ALIGN_8`, which the renderer centres. The alignment lives in the open callback, not in the item.

Measured after the fix: "Nouvelle partie" ink spans x 197..439 in the 640 box — **197 left, 200 right**. Centred.

## Two things that came out of it

**A screen's open callback sets flags its items don't carry.** `Ui.open_flags` now recovers those calls from the callback's bytes — same technique as `Opt_BindRow`'s row bindings — and `item_flags` applies them. That's general: it also picks up the `0x40000200` cursor-flag clears those callbacks do on every list.

**Alignment precedence, from `Text_LayOutBlock`'s order.** The markup is read *during* layout, after the parameter block is applied — so a `{C}` in a string beats the item's flags; with no directive the item's alignment stands; with neither, 2 (left). I had this backwards: I was passing the item's alignment as an override, which would have silently ignored a `{C}` in any string that had one.

`verify.py: ui open flags` pins it by measuring the rendered margins, so it can't drift back.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
- I2D 2D layer: 16-layer display list (4862 nodes), 7 primitives with typed pools, DirectDraw `Blt` back end with colour-key (not alpha) transparency, bitmap cache
- Widget tree: screen (124B, 3 slots at 0x4E9818) → panel → up to 10 lists → items (72B); four flag banks selected by the top bits of a flag constant
- 37-screen definition table (0x004CB640, 92B), 45 interface sounds (0x004D0990, 20B), 74 option items (0x004DA574, 140B), 13 options pages (0x004DD3D0, 104B), 8 oscillators (0x004C3EA0, 40B), 13 fonts (0x004C7090, 20B)
- `.FNT`: 256 8-byte glyph records + pixels from byte 2048; offsets in eight-byte units; pixel = coverage 0..31 into a 32-entry colour ramp
- Text markup: `{f<letter>}` font, `{I<9 decimal digits>}` colour, `{X<6>}` position %, `{C}/{D}/{F}/{G}` align, `{H}/{L}/{M}` valign, `{B}` blink, `[...]` counted spans; unrecognised letter = line flush
- Input: 14 binding slots, bit 1<<k, shared with `.CTL`; edge-trigger mask 0x203F; 4 context groups × 14 actions × 3 devices
- Fight AI in `.CTL` `+76`/`+80`: 156-byte profiles, moves = sequences of input words injected via `Perso_InjectInput`
- Headless simulator (`tools/sim/`), golden traces, `verify.py` as the corpus gate
- Extraction traps: functions absent from `Runtime.exe.c` with no `proc` label; `asmfn.py` returning wrong blocks; case-sensitive globs

ALIGN = {"G": 2, "D": 4, "C": 8, "F": 16}      # 4 = right, 8 = centre, else left

- **Miscounted 3 vs 6 gate-8 recipes**; the check caught it.
- **Case-sensitive glob** found 5 `.CTL` files instead of 7, missing two of three AI profile sets → globbed both cases; the check now says why.
- **Miscounted "21 open / 11 close" callbacks** (included the nulls) → 20 and 10.
- **Overstated "walks every interface panel"** in CLAUDE.md → corrected to five panels; added `sim: ui coverage`.
- **Model answered right for the wrong reason**: I moved between lists on left/right; the engine uses the panel hook with up/down. Fixed by adding `PANEL_HOOKS` and the `approx` flag.
- **Cutscene list empty**: I first blamed my own `pkill -f omkweb.py` (which did kill the user's server, but wasn't the cause). User said "the cutscene list is still empty". Real cause: a backtick inside a comment inside the GLSL template literal, closing it early; valid JS so `node --check` passed, threw `ReferenceError: clock` in `initGL`. Found by running the script under node with a DOM stub. Added `verify.py: page templates`.
- **Text invisible on three screens**: I spent a long diagnosis on the cache stamp. **User: "Stop doing overkilled things, it is just width/height issue of the img tag"** — correct: `.stage img{...width:640px;height:480px}` matched every img. Fixed by scoping to `.stage img.bg`. Recorded in CLAUDE.md §5 with the lesson: when an element is present and correct in the DOM but paints wrong, the stylesheet is the first place to look.
- **`page cache busting` check's first version** was wrong twice: a flat regex truncated a URL at the `"` inside `${clip.split("|")[0]}` (false positive), then treating apostrophes in prose comments as string delimiters desynchronised the scan so it caught nothing. Fixed by skipping comments first.
- **Start menu text left-aligned**: items store bank C as zero; `Ui_OpenStartMenu` broadcasts `0x80000010`. Fixed via `open_flags`/`item_flags`; also fixed alignment precedence so markup `{C}` beats the item's flags.

## What the menu capture turned out to be

The design question came first: `ui.open`'s `.TAG` domain is `None` — the handler announces nothing — so **no keystroke can ever appear in a trace**. A menu is visible only through what the *script* does around it. That framing is what makes the captures worth anything.

**Two new traces**, both from `AREA 118 +4` — the boot area's script and the only one in the game that opens `OMK START MENU`:

- `menu-noinput.log` — the **suspension**: exactly the three operands before `ui.open`, then 60s of silence. Which three is *predicted* by `goldentrace.loggable` from the decode, not asserted.
- `menu-keys.log` — the **reopen**, and it's a correction: `return,down,return` makes the preamble repeat **four times with nothing between** — no camera, never `Interface`. The script is restarted, not resumed. The widget model expects the opposite ("Nouvelle partie" has no `+40` callback, so `_confirm` should enter its `+44` sub-panel silently). Why, I did not establish, and said so.

## What the confirm path turned out to be

`Ui_ConfirmSelection` (`0x0042A750`) runs the item's `+40` callback, else enters its `+44` panel **and runs that panel's builder at `+4`** — the piece the sim didn't model. For "Nouvelle partie" that builder is `0x0047A050`, which **clears the name buffer** and zeroes the cursor. Then `Confirmer` opens:

```
0047A2B0  mov  eax, [dword_657994]   ; the name field's cursor
0047A2B6  test eax, eax
0047A2B9  je   0x0047A35E            ; empty name -> straight to the ret
```

Both writes that make an answer happen — `mov [esi+8], 3` (close the screen) and `mov dword_930750, 1` (the answer) — sit **below** that branch. So confirming with an empty field writes nothing, the screen stays open, and the calling script stays suspended at `ui.open` for ever.

**That is exactly what yesterday's capture showed.** A scripted `return,down,return` never types, so it never *could* have answered. The mechanism I left as "not established" is now closed from the code. There's a second refusal one branch on: a **duplicate** name forces `eax = -1` and is silently refused the same way.

**The simulator was wrong.** `ANSWER = {0x0047A2B0: 1}` was unconditional — the walker would have started a new game from a field the engine refuses. It now carries `ANSWER_NEEDS_NAME`, `Ui.name`/`type_name`, and `ui_answer` types a name because typing is as much the player's half as the presses. Three checks now assert **both** arms (1 with a name, nothing without), where before they only knew one.

Two corrections to my own earlier write-up, which mattered:

- I'd claimed the preamble's repeat count "tracked the RETURNs that landed". It doesn't — four identical runs gave 1, 2, 3, 4 copies, and the capture has **no unique anchor**, so even attributing the block to `AREA 118 +4` rests on a prefix match. Now recorded as an open observation, and the check asserts the count only as a property of the stored file.
- I chased an append-the-log theory, tested it with two identical runs, and it was **refuted** (`CX_LOG` truncates). Worth the two minutes — it was the only explanation that would have made the counts meaningless artifacts.

Also named the 14 start-menu panel callbacks in `ui_tables.CALLBACKS` (all absent from the decompilation — no `push` prologue), and added `ui confirm gate`, which pins the branch as raw bytes rather than through `asmfn.py`, which would silently return the neighbouring block.

The `Interface == 0` arm remains uncaptured — §4.6's standing gap, unchanged.

**Claude**

No — the main loop was done in **phase 3**, back on 2026-08-28. It's split across two levels, and only the outer shell is phase-5-shaped:

```
WinMain              cmdline flags: window / nofmv / config
 └ Game_Main         0x00439470  12_win32.c  — three FLIS intro movies,
                                              then Game_Start("aventure.scx")
   └ Game_RunLoop    0x00439310  12_win32.c  — the message pump; PeekMessage/
                                              WaitMessage, ESC → UI screen 31
     └ Game_Frame    0x0041F740  05_sys.c    — the master clock
       └ Game_Tick   0x004200F0  05_sys.c    — contexts, programs, wait scan
```

All four are `NAMED`, none `CLEAN`. `Game_RunLoop` is the only genuinely platform-layer piece, and it's already read — 46 lines, and there's nothing left in it to discover.

The interesting half is squarely game core. `Game_Frame` owns the clock: `flt_4C30D8` is the frame delta in **30 fps units** (30/fps clamped to 3.0), with debug speed modes 1.0/0.5/0.1/2.0 and `dword_4E9728` the pause flag forcing dt to 0 — and **while a morph plays the dt is slaved to the morph's audio-position clock**, so the whole engine follows the spoken line's audio. That's the single most load-bearing fact in the loop: it's what confirmed the viewer's timing model at the top level, and it's why the cutscene clock counts frames rather than seconds.

`Game_Tick` is where the frame pacing was closed on 2026-08-29 — the wait-slot scan (`dword_910500/4/8`) that makes a finishing cutscene beat advance the next one. `tools/sim` reproduces `Game_Tick`'s order exactly: contexts, programs, wait scan.

So phase 5 is DirectX, win32 and OLE plumbing *around* the loop, not the loop itself — and the plan says identify-and-name only, transcribe only if level C is attempted. The loop was never going to sit there; it's the seam between the platform and the game, and the game side of it was needed before the simulator could run at all.

## The one thing genuinely missing

**The tables compiled into `Runtime.exe` are not extracted.** `tab_special_move` (66 rows), the camera-mode presets, the weapon stats, the key bindings, the ADPCM tables, the opcode operand lengths. A replica that asks the user for their own game data will **not find these in `fr/`** — they live in the executable. The plan deliberately deferred it ("doing it now only creates a second copy to drift") — that reason expires the moment `engine/` exists. This is the single hard prerequisite.

## Mandatory for a first slice

Taking the slice as *boot → new game → stand in a set → walk → trip a zone → have a conversation*:

| piece | why mandatory | what you port from |
|---|---|---|
| **the clock** | `Game_Frame`: dt in 30 fps units (30/fps clamped to 3.0), pause forces 0, and **while a morph plays dt is slaved to the morph's audio clock**. Then `Game_Tick`'s order: contexts, programs, wait scan. Get this wrong and everything downstream desyncs silently | read; `tools/sim` reproduces the order |
| **file readers** | all of them — IAM, .3DO, .3DT, .3DM, .ani, .CTL, .3DA, .3DP, .SCX, .SFX, DIALOG, START | **write fresh**, prove byte-identical against the Python over every shipped file |
| **the 8192-byte game DB** | the VM writes to it; `IAM\START` *is* the new-game save | `GameDB` is already a real struct in `readable/types.h` |
| **the VM** | ~15 opcodes need real semantics; the rest stub-and-log and control flow stays correct | `tools/sim/vm.py` + the golden traces |
| **scheduler, zones, events** | without it nothing starts — entering an area runs the chunk's `+4` script | `tools/sim/world.py` |
| **area/scene load** | `+4` startup script, `+88` set, `+97` scene script | `tools/sim/run.py` |
| **actor + walker** | ground probe, 30 cm step, ledge refusal, gravity | `tools/sim/actor.py` |
| **renderer, minimal** | drawable mask `flags & 0x800043`; bucket key ascending; blend modes; per-vertex colour as D3DCOLOR; `W(v)=[x,−y,z]` with the projection negating X | all settled, each with a check |
| **ADPCM** | already transcribed from `sub_483200` | tier-3 kernel, provable |

Skippable for v1: the 58-slot texture cache (the viewers are *right* and the game is the odd one out — reproducing it means reproducing a bug), the 37-screen UI (load `IAM\START` directly instead of walking the start menu), combat, inventory.

## What is mandatory *not* to do

No original assembly, no static recompilation, no porting the six x87 rasterizers / DirectX / win32 / C runtime — 695 functions and 45k lines explicitly out of scope. And **never paste from `readable/`**: it holds ~15100 offset accessors against the original 32-bit image. Turning those offsets into fields *is* the port.

## The honest caveats

- **84 sites where the decompiler admits it dropped a conditional**, plus 204 possibly-undefined variables. Wherever you hit one, `Runtime.exe.asm` is the only honest source.
- Only **64 functions are CLEAN**. That's less limiting than it sounds — the 2026-08-30 refinement says CLEAN is required only where the port *can't* be proved independently (input, render state, fight AI). Formats, kernels, the VM and most runtime behaviour prove against the corpus and the traces instead.
- The narrow-phase sweep kernel (930 lines of x87) has **no shipped fact to prove a transcription against**. `tools/sim` implements the algorithm's shape, not the kernel. Fine for a first version; know that it's the one place the standard is already relaxed.

Want me to do the table extraction? It's the only blocking item, it's bounded, and every table already has a check to validate the lift against.

| | whole binary | game code only |

| `operator new` / `delete` | 12 / 17 | mostly runtime |

So the game itself has no classes, no virtual dispatch, no STL, no exceptions. Its idiom is structs, free functions, and tables of function pointers. You wouldn't be departing from a C++ design — there isn't one.

**Which means: use C++, and I think it's the better choice on the merits.** Three concrete reasons, not just taste:

1. **The single biggest porting hazard is the ~15100 offset accessors** (`u32(p, 12)`) becoming real fields. Strong typing is exactly the tool for that, and `readable/types.h`'s 17 structs map straight over. A silent field-offset error is the failure mode this port will actually have.
2. **Every format is "load the whole file, relocate offsets to pointers in place"** — that's an ownership problem, and RAII with `vector<byte>` plus spans is strictly better than reproducing the engine's manual `Mem_Free` discipline.
3. Differential testing against the Python readers wants a test framework and easy binary comparison.

**Where I'd keep it deliberately plain**, and I'd hold this line:

- **The VM's 153 opcodes**: a switch or an array of function pointers, indexed to match `tables/vm_opcodes.json`. Not 153 classes. That table is *data* we extracted today and can diff against; turning it into a hierarchy breaks the correspondence.
- **`tab_special_move`'s 66 rows, the camera presets, the key bindings**: arrays, for the same reason.
- **Hot loops** — the 0x4000-bucket render walk, the vertex transform, `Sweep_PolygonKernel`. Data-oriented, structs-of-arrays. A virtual call per face would be wrong on both speed and clarity.
- **Floats**: the decompilation is full of `double` temporaries because x87 promotes everything — that's an artifact, not intent. Use `float` where the data is float, and don't enable `-ffast-math`; the plan already accepts low-bit drift, but you don't want to add more.

The one real risk with OOP here: it can obscure the correspondence to `readable/`. When behaviour diverges you'll want to compare against a CLEAN body function by function, and deep inheritance makes that mapping harder. So keep the *decomposition* close to the engine's — one module per subsystem, functions carrying the engine's own names — even where the implementation is idiomatic C++. That costs nothing and preserves your ability to diff.

Shall I start the `.3DT` slice that way — `engine/` with a small C++ reader and a `verify.py` check diffing it against `tex3dt.py` over all 2534 textures?

## What made it reach past the conversation

`dialog.start` **doesn't suspend its context**. The handler leaves it running with the pc past the operand, `Script_Execute` returns for the frame, and `g_DialogState` goes to 3 — after which the pump refuses to run until case 63 puts it back. The world stops *around* the launch script and it resumes at the next instruction **with its stack intact**. That's why a context now owns its interpreter rather than getting a fresh one each frame.

Both filters applied to the comparison are the engine's own: `Dbg_LogTagged` drops `a1 == -1`, the `CHARACTERS` domain and `VALUES` before the profile call, so a diff must apply the same three or it reports the logger's filter as a disagreement.

## The mistake worth reporting

I hand-wrote the announce map — which `.TAG` domain each opcode narrates to — from what looked plausible. It was **wrong three ways within the hour**: `scx.play` and `music.play` announce *nothing*, and `scx.play.actor.wait` announces the **actor**, not the object. Three phantom events in a 14-event sequence.

That's CLAUDE.md §1's rule biting inside the port itself, so I fixed the cause rather than the symptom: `tables/vm_announce.json` is now generated from the assembly by `tools/vm_announce.py` and loaded as data — 49 handlers announce, 104 are silent, and `field` says *which* operand (`scene.load` announces its second). I've also flagged in `tables/README.md` that this one table has a different provenance from the other six: they're read out of the executable's bytes, this one from the disassembly.

Without that fix the check would have been comparing my guesses against the engine and quietly failing on three of fourteen.

## This slice: `.CTL` state machines

The biggest single port so far, and the one with the sharpest invariant. A `.CTL` is a **byte walk**: a fixed header, entries, then nine variable-length sections in a fixed order, each present only when a flag on the entry says so. Nothing points at the next section — the reader adds up the sizes.

That makes **"the walk lands exactly on the file size" the entire proof**, not a tidiness check. Misread one gate — the `0x8002` unnamed junction, the `0x140` turn, the `0x280` root shift, the `0x2000000` combat window, the fight-AI table's two-pass layout — and everything after it is out of step. **All 7 shipped files land exactly.**

Then the graph, independently: **398 clips, 1286 states, 1113 gotos, 0 unresolved of any kind.**

## A number worth resolving rather than accepting

My edge count came out **1862** against the documented **931**. That's not a discrepancy: children and parents are the *same* edges stored both ways, so 931 distinct = 1862 stored. The reference confirms it — 931 children + 931 parents. And 931 + 1113 gotos = the 2044 the docs quote. I've written the reconciliation into the check so the next person doesn't have to re-derive it.

Also carried across: the format's trailing pointer fields are **dead**. `InitCEFFile` never follows them, it recomputes them — and chasing them is what made this format look unsolvable. A port that trusted them would read garbage, so the header says so explicitly.

Two things a reader gets wrong unless told, and I've put both in the header so the next person doesn't rediscover them:

The interpreter deliberately **reproduces a bug rather than fixing it**: the loop rewind goes through `Script_StartScript`, which zeroes the `loopsDone` it just tested, so a finite loop count above 1 would loop for ever. It never bites because the data uses only 1 and −1 — and the engine's behaviour is the specification, so it is modelled and the reason is written down.

## The boot sequence — `docs/BOOT.md`

```
WinMain            WINDOW · NOFMV · CONFIG
  Game_Main        (the whole thing inside one setjmp3; the else arm is "Can't initialize")
    Game_Init
    Movie_Play FLIS\EIDOS.mpg / QUANTIC.mpg / GAME.mpg
    Game_Start("aventure.scx")        ← the main menu is a SCENE, not a state
    Game_RunLoop
```

Three things came out of reading it that weren't written down anywhere:

**I got the skip wrong last turn, and the truth is better.** There are *two* skips. `sub_439730` is the poll callback every `Movie_Play` gets: any key stops the movie playing, but only `Input_Poll` code **2** sets the latch that drops the rest — and code 2 is scan code **56**, `DIK_LMENU`. So any key skips one, **left Alt skips all three**. (The loop doesn't break on a hit either, so a key above scan code 56 held with Alt overwrites the 2 back to a 1 — Alt+Shift skips one.)

**The boot path is the first thing in the game that needs a case-insensitive filesystem** — before any asset. The executable spells `FLIS\EIDOS.mpg` in lower case; the disc ships `EIDOS.MPG`. Not one uppercase form appears in the image.

**A correction to `CLAUDE.md`.** It quoted "the engine's frame delta is `flt_4C30D8 dd 1.0`" — that's its *shipped* value. `Game_Frame` recomputes it every frame as **`30.0 / fps`, clamped at 3.0**. So the unit is a thirtieth of a second, which is *why* every clock in this repo counts frames — it isn't a convention anyone chose, it falls out of that one division. The clamp is a gameplay fact: below 10 fps the game slows down rather than taking bigger steps, so integrating true elapsed time on a slow machine is wrong, not more accurate. All seven constants read out of the image and pinned by `verify.py: boot sequence`.

## The Session loop

`scx.play*` was being recorded and dropped, so the interpreter I ported yesterday had nothing to start it. `SceneRunner` is the join, driven by both the zone lifecycle and the area session. Standing in zone 3732 now runs the whole chain in C++:

```
zone 3732 in SCENE 53 plays its objects from Re14.SCX
    scx.play.player object 22   Uzal---->assis   (the caller waits)
    scx.play.player object 32   Uzal_Stand
    dialog 387 with 13 nodes
    2 programs, 1 still running after 120 frames
```

Identical to `tools/sim/run.py` stage 4b, line for line. Two things there fail silently rather than loudly: the operand is an object id *local to the resident scene*, so resolving SCENE 53 → AREA 217 → `+97` wrong picks the wrong object with no error; and 59/60 name the **actor first and the object second**, so reading field 0 for all six variants starts the wrong thing on two of them.

The nicest part was unplanned. Booting AREA 118 with scenes on makes `Grid.SCX` resident — the title sequence's own — and it holds an object named **`Wait5sec`** whose single function is `Wait` with the parameter **150.0**. The name says five seconds, the number says 150. Someone authoring content in 1999 wrote the engine's time unit down, and it's the same `30.0 / fps` the boot doc arrived at from the executable.

## 1. The frustum, finished

`sub_48D0D0` read. **The engine builds no plane from an angle.** It takes the four corners of the view rectangle *at the far plane* —

```
(±far·w / (2·projX),  ±far·h / (2·projY),  far)
```

— viewport at camera `+0x19C`/`+0x19E`, projection scales at `+0xE4`/`+0xE8` — transforms them to world space, and hands the eye plus two adjacent corners to `sub_442FB0` four times, into `flt_660AD4 … flt_660B18` struct-of-arrays. **The two axes scale independently; there is no aspect-ratio term.** And the far distance I'd had to set aside is `dword_6A2B9C` = camera `+0x154`, with near at `+0x144` — both settled by the range test that rejects `z ≤ near` or `z ≥ far`.

**That vindicates an assertion I withdrew.** Yesterday four of Anekbah's meshes were kept at 45° and dropped at 90°, by margins of 84–457 units, and I concluded "widening the fov can only keep more" was untestable because it was a property of my fixture. It wasn't untestable — it was *true*, and the aspect-ratio term I'd invented was the bug. With the engine's construction it holds at 0 violations and is now asserted. The lesson is the §1 one from the other side: a plausible stand-in that fails an invariant is evidence against the stand-in, not against the invariant.

## 2. The actor runtime's `.CTL` half

The data the fight AI I ported last week actually drives — I'd ported the caller without the callee.

```
combat: 116 blocks, 232 reaction refs of which 232 resolve, 0 id collisions; damage 1..25
groups: 202, of which 202 have exactly one default entry; 7 files with right role codes
transitions: 1286 entries, 640 coded (28 no-input sentinels), 168 cancel windows (0 malformed)
```

Three things there are content rather than layout, which is what makes them tests:

- **The combat block's ten floats include three integers wearing float bytes.** Damage reads 1..25 by reinterpreting; converting gives 25.0f, which is not 25.
- **A reaction names a state by its low sixteen bits**, which works only because that id space is collision-free — 0 collisions in any file, and nothing in the format enforces it.
- **`Fight_Begin` caches six role codes** and every combat file carries exactly one entry of each, every non-combat file none: 7 of 7. A wrong offset wouldn't produce that shape.

But `tools/sim/ui.py` is deterministic and walks five panels with the engine's own input words — the start menu with its 20-character name field and empty-name gate, the confirm dialog, the LIFT's 7-slot grid, the options page tree, the load panel — and `verify.py: ui page` exercises every screen and key sequence with no server. That's a real oracle for the *logic*: given a key sequence, which item is focused and what answer comes out. Porting the widget tree, the 14-bit input word with its `0x203F` edge mask, and the panel→list→default dispatch would be diffable against it end to end. It converts "9 rows with no oracle" into "the UI decides identically; only the pixels are unverified."

**2. Text layout and `Text_DrawRun`.** The `.FNT` format is ported; the layout isn't. `tools/uitext.py` renders a line with the real fonts and markup, so a glyph-position differential is available — cheap, and it finishes the fonts slice properly.

**4. The 3776 unexplained radii.** Narrow, blocks nothing.

I'd do **1**. It's the largest genuinely-testable block left, and my reason for skipping it — "no oracle" — turns out to have been wrong: the simulator is the oracle, the same way it was for the scripts. **2** is the natural warm-up if you'd rather start small, since it's a couple of hours and closes a slice that's currently half-done.

**The tree had to be lifted first.** Panels, lists and items are `.data` in the executable, not in `fr/`, so `tables/ui_widgets.json` is now an eighth table — 28 panels, 71 lists, 361 items — re-derived by `exe tables` so it can't go stale. Its limit is recorded rather than papered over: a panel links to its *parent* at `+0` and never to a child, and child panels are installed by native code, so this is every screen's top panel only. That's why the start menu's name-field hook doesn't appear among the 31 hooked lists at all.

**The finding is a trap I walked into.** The open callback's `I2D_SetFlag` calls are recovered by scanning its bytes linearly — and callbacks have branches. The ten shop screens grey item 0 and enable item 1 on one arm and the reverse on the other, so a linear scan sees `off, off, on, on` for one item and `on, on, off, off` for its neighbour. Applying them in address order picks whichever arm comes last, and made item 0 unselectable on all ten. That was precisely the 10 screens where the two implementations disagreed.

**20 of the 361 items carry a flag written both ways.** Such a write is conditional and a linear scan can't resolve it, so it must be refused and the static record left standing — which is what the reference does by reading `+48` raw. Cruder, and right for the same reason. It's CLAUDE.md §1's "a regex must respect nesting" one level up: a linear byte scan over a branching function.

Two smaller things: `UI_GridMenuInput` is ported (the LIFT's floor panel — four DOWNs land on slot 4, and confirm answers `slot − 1` with slot 0 giving 6), and **`Ui_MoveBetweenLists` is deliberately left unwired**, because the reference transcribes it as `_move_lists` and then never calls it. Wiring it would have manufactured a disagreement; matching the reference is what makes the diff mean something.

Also added `src/platform/json.h` — a hundred-line JSON reader, since the flat `find("\"op\":")` scan the other tables use can't tell which nesting level a key belongs to.

**One correction to what I said an hour ago, though — I was too pessimistic about `ACTOR_STATE`.**

I said it would be "read and explained, not verified," because no capture announces an actor state. That's true about the *engine's behaviour*. But the data it drives is already ported and asserted, and that constrains the runtime quite hard:

- every state the machine enters must be a real `.CTL` entry, and all 2044 graph edges already resolve;
- every transition it takes must be one the entry's `+4` input code and priority actually allow — 1286 entries, 640 with an input word, priorities only 0/1/2;
- a landed hit must resolve to a reaction state by its low 16 bits, and that id space is collision-free in all 7 files;
- the AI's injected input words are a known set (bit union `0xCFF`), so a machine that reaches a state no profile can ask for is wrong;
- combat files carry exactly one entry of each of `Fight_Begin`'s six role codes, so the machine's entry points are pinned.

So it's not verifiable against the game, but it's very far from unfalsifiable — the same move as "make the parse self-checking," applied to a runtime. I'd tell the next session to build those invariants first and the machine second, and to say in the header that the standard is *data-constrained*, not *engine-verified*. Those are different claims and the difference should be visible in the file rather than in someone's memory.

## 3. PORTING B6's audio row — and the criterion was wrong

**The engine does not mix.** `Sound_Init` (0x0046C3A0) creates a DirectSound *primary* buffer, sets it to PCM/2ch/**22050**/16/align 4/88200, and calls `Play(0,0,LOOPING)` once; everything after is a *secondary* buffer DirectSound sums in. No loop in the image adds two samples together, so "the mix compared offline" could never have been met. Corrected in B6 and A5 rather than left looking unfinished — the engine's half is **decisions**, which is A2's boundary unchanged.

`engine/src/audio/mixer.*` + `run_audio` + `verify.py: engine audio`. Ported: `Wav_LoadToBuffer` accepting **all 61** shipped `.wav`, `Sound_LengthMs` differenced against a Python re-derivation, the 160-buffer bank, the 16-voice pool and its flag word, `Sound_FreeBuffer` killing what plays it, the listener, the volume law.

Four things the reading produced:

- **The volume "percentage" is an attenuation** — `-10000*pct/100`, so 0 is full and 100 is silence, and the global initialises to 0.
- **The listener is told the world unit is an inch** — `flDistanceFactor = 0x3CD013A9 = 0.0254`. Its argument is in the engine's order (position, top, front, velocity), not `DS3DLISTENER`'s, so a straight copy swaps orientation for velocity.
- **The interface caches 32 of its 45 sounds.** `Ui_LoadSound` takes the first free slot and **returns silently** when there is none, so 13 can never be resident. 16 further `.wav` ship unnamed, one called `cptrebour02..wav`.
- **Three more functions absent from the decompilation** — `Sound_SetFrequency` (0x0046CBF0), `Sound_GetFrequency` (0x0046CC30), `Sound_LengthMs` (0x0046CC70). All open `mov eax, ds:ppDS` with no `push` prologue. §1's trap, first time in the audio module.

Two of `Wav_LoadToBuffer`'s branches are **dead against the corpus** (all 61 take the two-byte-peek rewind; 0 skip a chunk). The one waveform claim, met: `men001.wav` comes out **sample-identical in both channels over 32953 frames**, with the FNV recomputed in `verify.py` from the file so the identity is across the two implementations; `pause.wav` at **22080 Hz** is the control and 33572 of 34323 frames differ. **The attenuation and pan law is DirectSound's and has no reachable tier** — said in `mixer.h`, in `render()` and in the coverage row.

All six mutations were run: rewind dropped → 61 accepted becomes **0**; first `"sounds"` key → **0 names** (it did, and the check passed until the count was asserted); no resample → `pause` 33572 → **0**; listener guard → 1 → **0**; `freeBuffer` not killing voices → 0 → **4**. The sixth, `nBlockAlign` for `(bits/8)*channels`, **moves nothing** — recorded as non-discriminating (B7) rather than counted as evidence.

Coverage: **31 fully, 7 partly, 0 lifted-unconsumed** — the 45 interface sounds were the last row in that bucket.

`python3 tools/verify.py --slow` → **198 checks, 0 failed** (8m27s).

## 13. User  ·  2026-09-01 13:13:58

Ok, should we continue with the Vulkan back-end, or should we do something else before?


**Claude**

Let me check one thing so the recommendation isn't hand-waving — what the 3D side already has, and what it lacks:

> `Bash` — What the 3D side has and lacks


**Claude**

**Not Vulkan yet — the software 3D rasterizer first.** That's not my preference, it's what your own standard says, and building Vulkan now would break it.

## Why

`PORTING` A4 is explicit that the software backend comes first, and gives three reasons. Two of them bite hard right now:

- **"It is the only path the oracle can check."** A Vulkan frame can't be diffed against `traces/frames/` in any strong sense — different rasterisation rules, filtering, precision.
- **"It separates two kinds of bug."** With Vulkan first, a wrong-looking frame is either a wrong *ported decision* or a wrong *API call*, and telling them apart is expensive exactly when the code is newest.

And B6's own Vulkan row says its correctness is **"inherited from the software backend it mirrors"**. For 3D, that backend doesn't exist — so Vulkan would inherit from nothing. The 2D half is done (blits 66560/66560, quad 1518/1518, text 6132/6132); the 3D half has **no rasterizer at all**, and can't have a ported one, because I established earlier this session that the engine's mode-2 rasterizers are 2D only and its 3D path is D3D in every mode.

## What's already there, and what's missing

Everything *except* the pixels. `src/o3de/` has the drawable mask, the 14-bit bucket key, the two blend modes and the cutout, the 58-slot texture cache, `cullMesh` and the frustum — the whole decision layer, checked. Geometry, textures, cameras and the visible-set walk are ported. `Surface` has **zero** occurrences of depth, texel or UV: nothing turns a submitted triangle into pixels.

So the missing piece is one reference implementation — a textured, vertex-coloured, z-buffered triangle into the RGB565 framebuffer, honouring the blend modes the decisions already produce. Like `render()` in the mixer and `movie.cpp`, it's not a port of anything; it stands where D3D stood.

## And it unlocks what you already asked for

You said the panel issue "will be easier to check once we will have a render" — that's exactly where this lands. **Anekbah's shop signs** is the repo's oldest unfalsified prediction, explicitly labelled *falsifiable by playing*, and it's the one place the docs claim the viewers are right and the game is the odd one out. With a renderer, walking in from two different neighbours and comparing the sign becomes a check rather than an inference. It also gives the frame oracle something beyond the menu.

**My recommendation:** software 3D rasterizer next, then Anekbah as its first real test, then Vulkan mirroring a backend that has actually been checked.

The one thing that would change my mind is if you want something *playable-looking* sooner and are willing to accept it unverified — Vulkan would get a textured world on screen faster. But it would be the first slice in this tree with no evidence behind it, and I'd rather you chose that deliberately than drift into it.

didn't you said earlier that the game doesn't have his own rasterizer?

**Claude**

**Claude**

No contradiction, but you've caught that my *reason* was partly wrong — and re-reading it, I'd closed a row I shouldn't have. Both are now fixed.

## Squaring the two statements

Both are true, and they're about different things:

- **The game has two rasterizers of its own** — `sub_48C4C0` (Bresenham) and `sub_48C060` (box fill). Both are **2D**, both are ported, both at tier 4.
- **It has no 3D rasterizer.** Direct3D drew every triangle; nothing in the 3D path branches on the driver mode.

So a software 3D rasterizer in the replica is **new code, not a transcription**. And that matters for the argument I gave you: `PORTING` A4's *first* reason for doing the software backend first is **"It is the port — the rasterizers have to be read and transcribed regardless."** For 3D that reason **does not apply**, and it was my own finding that removed it. I quoted A4 at you without noticing I'd invalidated a third of it.

## And I over-closed the B6 row

I closed the rasterizer row arguing "a captured 3D frame would verify Wine, not the port." That's too strong, and B5 already says why: a capture is **"exact about geometry and ordering, and not about a pixel's low bits."** Geometry and ordering *are* the port's business — the visible-set walk, the bucket order, the transforms, the culling, all of which are ported and currently checked **only against themselves**. I threw away a live criterion.

B6 now has two rows instead of one: the 2D rasterizers (met), and a new **3D rasterizer** row — a reference implementation, not a port, with the criterion restored as *silhouette and coverage against a captured 3D frame; per-pixel equality is not the criterion*.

## So does the recommendation survive?

Yes, but on two legs instead of three:

- **A4 reason 3 — separating bug kinds.** A software rasterizer is deterministic, headless, and runs inside `verify.py`. With Vulkan first, a wrong frame is either a wrong ported decision or a wrong API call, and that ambiguity is worst when the code is newest.
- **A4 reason 2, weakened but real.** Only the software path can be diffed against a capture at all in this suite, and only it can check the geometry-and-ordering claim above.

Vulkan has exactly the same evidential standing as the software path for *pixels* (neither can claim them) but a worse one for *everything else*, and B6 still says its correctness is inherited from the backend it mirrors.

**So: software 3D rasterizer first — but as a declared reference implementation, not as "the port".** That's the honest framing, and it's the one thing my earlier answer got wrong.

## The Makefile first, since it was the real cost

`engine/Makefile` now compiles to `build/obj/**.o` with `-MMD -MP` and links. The old rule built each tool from `tools/%.cpp $(SRC)` in one command — ~37 tools × ~40 sources ≈ **1500 translation units per build** — and made every binary depend on `$(HDRS)`, so touching any header rebuilt everything. `verify.py` runs `make -s` once per engine check, so the suite paid it too.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| clean build | ~6 min | **10.8 s** |
| no-op | ~6 min | **0.027 s** |
| one source edited | ~6 min | **0.67 s** |
| one header edited | ~6 min | **2.0 s** |

Binaries produce identical numbers. Header deps are now per-object and exact, which is *more* correct than the blanket `$(HDRS)`, not just faster; `-MP` keeps a deleted header from wedging the build. Parallel by default (`-j$(nproc)`), override with `-j1`.

## The I2D port

`engine/src/ui/i2d.{h,cpp}` + `engine/tools/run_i2d.cpp` + `verify.py: engine I2D` (0.76 s). The DirectDraw back end isn't ported and can't be from here — `Blt` is on the far side of the same line as the rasterizers. What is ported is what the layer **decides**: the display list, the seven pools, every acceptance test, the three flag banks.

**Two documented readings were wrong.**

- **The per-layer cache is a HEAD cache, not the "tail cache" `docs/UI.md` described.** The assembly writes `dword_4E97B8[layer]` on both exits of the list walk and *not* on the cache-hit path, which only does `new->next = cached->next; cached->next = new`. So **within one layer the first primitive submitted draws first and the rest draw in reverse submission order.** A real tail cache scores 724/1407 against the prediction instead of 1407 — right about every layer boundary, wrong about every overlap inside one, and no screenshot would say which.
- **The 4862-node cap is the sum of the seven pools** (4096+200+100+220+220+16+10) — and that only closes if you count the pool of a primitive **nothing calls**. `sub_428660` (cap 10) and `sub_4286F0` have no callers, and the second carries a latent overflow: it checks the 220-entry bitmap counter and writes the 10-entry pool. Kept, not fixed.

**A third thing the check found rather than the reading:** the frame's first node takes `I2D_Enqueue`'s `if (!count)` arm and sets no cache, so its layer orders `s1, s(n-1)…s2, s0`. My first version predicted one shape and scored 1260/1407 — the 147 misses were exactly the layers holding node 0.

Also: **both blits apply three rectangle tests, not four — there's no test on the source Y**, identically in both. A source inverted only vertically is submitted. Asserted rather than tidied away; "fixing" it takes the count 2 → 0.

**The one data-falsifiable check**, and I've said in the header and the docstring that it's the only one: the widget tree ships **139 flag constants** and `I2D_SetFlag` silently drops any that names no bank. All 139 resolve, 42/95/2 across the three words. Breaking the `0x40000000` test takes it to 44. All three falsifications confirmed.

Coverage is now 30 fully ported, **6 partly**, 2 lifted-unconsumed, **0 wholly unported**, 3 instruments. What's left is all output: DirectDraw, the rasterizers, `Text_DrawRun`, audio, and the 26 screen callbacks absent from the decompilation.

Here's what I'd write, before I write it.

## `docs/PORTING.md` — the porting standard

**Why a new doc, not a CLAUDE.md section:** CLAUDE.md §1 is the working practice for *reading* the game (data proposes, code decides). This is the working practice for *porting* it, which is a different discipline and has been accumulating unstated. RECONSTRUCTION.md is the plan and the log; this is the rule the log is judged against.

**1. The evidence ladder.** Six tiers, each with its meaning, a shipped example, and — the part that matters — what it does *not* license you to claim:

| | example |
|---|---|
| exact bytes | `.3DT` 2534/2534 |
| corpus-constrained | `.CTL` 7/7 landing on the file size |
| differential | `tools/sim`, `adp.py` |
| behavioural | golden traces 42/42; **and now the framebuffer** |
| data-constrained | `ACTOR_STATE` — the data it reads is checkable, the logic isn't |
| read and explained | I2D's ordering, the shoot AI's state graphs |

It's descriptive of what's already there, which is why it can be written with confidence rather than invented.

**2. The declaration rule.** Every slice states its tier in three places — the source header, the check docstring, the coverage row. A green tick in `verify.py` otherwise implies more than was established, which is precisely how "no data at all" survived in the shoot AI docs.

**3. Four requirements per slice:** tier declared; oracle named or "none, and why none is possible"; at least one invariant the *shipped data* could fail, or an explicit statement there is none; and a falsification record.

**4. Falsification as a rule, not a habit.** Every check must be shown to fail. This earned its keep four times today — the circular dispatch check that passed while testing nothing, the driver bug that made 90 of 144 Gandhar steps disagree, the 147 ordering misses that turned out to be a second real shape, and the wrong-font IoU collapse.

**5. What the frame oracle licenses.** The 2D/3D split, the determinism caveat (text and the title yes, the animated scene no), and the refusal rule.

**6. Per remaining item: reachable tier and acceptance criterion** — what "done" means for `Text_DrawRun`, the 26 callbacks, the rasterizers, DirectDraw, audio, input.

**7. Anti-patterns** — things that look like evidence and aren't: two implementations of one reading agreeing; asking the code that made a decision whether it made it right; a corpus test that can't separate the rule from a simpler one (the priority rule, indistinguishable on all 120 contests); a count that's quietly short (708 `.3DM`, the eight `.SFX`).

One caveat I'd write into it: this is derived from what has worked, not decreed. When an instrument changes, the standard changes — which is exactly what happened this afternoon.

> `AskUserQuestion` — 


**Claude**

## Part A — target and architecture (missing)

Where I can now give a concrete answer:

- **Target: an offscreen software framebuffer, no platform API in `engine/`.** Not a fallback — the right answer. DirectDraw's `Blt` is a memory copy with an optional colour key, so software isn't an approximation of it, it *is* it. The six x87 rasterizers are software by definition. It keeps "no dependencies". And decisively: it's the only target that can be diffed against `traces/frames/` — an SDL window can't be, without adding a capture path to compare against a capture.
- **Pixel format: RGB565**, per above.
- **Audio: decode to PCM buffers, compare sample-exact.** Exactly the pattern ADPCM already uses (777/777 sample-identical). No audio device.
- **Input: replay of key events, not a device.** The binding tables are already lifted.
- **Timing: already settled** — the 30/fps frame delta, one unit is one frame.

Genuinely open, and not mine to default:

- **The 3D backend.** The D3D path is the one part that used hardware. A software rasterizer is exact and diffable but slow; a GPU backend is fast but forfeits pixel fidelity, leaving only geometry and ordering — which is, notably, all the frame oracle licenses for 3D anyway.
- **Float precision.** The original computes on the x87 stack at 80 bits. Golden traces sidestep this by diffing integers; a *pixel* diff of 3D can't. Needs a stated policy rather than a discovery.
- **Whether `engine/` ever becomes interactive.** Everything today is batch. If a window is never a goal, a lot of the above simplifies and the backend interface can be much narrower.

## Part B — evidence

The ladder, the declaration rule, the four requirements, falsification, what the frame licenses, the anti-patterns — as proposed, which you've approved.

Two questions decide Part A's shape:

> `AskUserQuestion` — 


**Claude**

Honest view, since you asked.

**Vulkan + MoltenVK is the right call for the playable target, and multi-backend is right full stop.** Your reasoning about OpenGL on macOS is correct — deprecated since 10.14, capped at 4.1, and the drivers are as bad as you say. If you're picking one modern cross-platform API, that's the one. MoltenVK's gaps (no geometry shaders, some format limits) don't touch anything a 1999 fixed-function game needs.

Two things I'd add, and one I'd argue about.

**The boundary belongs at the decision level, not the API level.** The engine already ports render *decisions* — the drawable mask `flags & 0x800043`, the 14-bit bucket key, the two blend modes, the 58-slot texture cache. The interface should take those ("draw this mesh, texture slot 37, additive, bucket key K"), not triangles-and-state. Get that right and both backends are additive and neither contaminates the ported code. Get it wrong — boundary at the Vulkan level — and the ported decisions leak into API code and the software path becomes impossible to add later.

**RGB565 needs to survive onto the GPU.** You'd naturally render to RGBA8. If the Vulkan path is ever to be compared against the software path or the captures, it needs to target a 565-equivalent format or quantise on readback. Cheap if specified now, annoying to retrofit.

**Where I'd push back: I'd write the software backend first — not instead.** Three reasons, none of them conservatism:

1. **It isn't extra work.** The six x87 rasterizers have to be read and ported regardless. Writing them into a framebuffer *is* that port. The Vulkan backend is entirely additional code — a few thousand lines that aren't a port of anything in the binary.
2. **It's the only path the oracle can check.** A software frame diffs against `traces/frames/` exactly. A Vulkan frame can't, in any strong sense — different rasterisation rules, filtering, precision.
3. **This is the one that actually costs you.** If Vulkan comes first and a frame looks wrong, you cannot tell whether the bug is in the *ported decisions* or in your Vulkan. With a verified software path you can, because it's exact. That ambiguity is expensive to debug and it lands exactly when the code is newest.

That said — if part of the point is getting Vulkan experience on real devices, that's a legitimate goal this repo's verification story has nothing to say about, and I'm not going to argue you out of it. My argument is only about *order*, and it's that software-first is roughly free and makes the Vulkan output trustworthy when it lands.

**On playability as a goal** — accepted, and it does reorder things. Worth knowing: a playable *menu* is close, since I2D, the widget tree, the text and the input words are ported and the frame oracle now covers them. A playable *game* needs the actor runtime, walker, collision and scene runtime running together in real time, which is a lot of already-ported code that has never been run as a loop.

So Part A would specify: the `Renderer` interface at decision level; RGB565 as the reference format on both paths; software backend as the reference implementation; Vulkan/MoltenVK as the playable backend; audio decoded to PCM with an optional device; input as replayable events with an optional live source. One boundary, two implementations each.

> `AskUserQuestion` — 


**Claude**

## `docs/PORTING.md` — written

**Part A — the target**, which is the half you identified as missing:

- **The renderer boundary sits at the decision level, not the API level.** It takes bucket key, drawable mask, blend mode, texture slot — what's actually been ported — and a backend turns those into API calls, never makes one. Put the boundary at Vulkan instead and the ported decisions leak into API code, the software path can't be added later, and the frame oracle becomes unusable.
- **RGB565**, measured rather than assumed — 32 red levels, 63 green, gaps of 8/9 and 4/5.
- **Software backend first, Vulkan/MoltenVK next**, with the argument recorded so it can be revisited rather than re-litigated.
- Audio as PCM compared sample-exact, input as a replayable event stream, each with an optional live device behind the same boundary.
- **Nothing `verify.py` touches may require an SDK** — if `make` ever needs Vulkan to build `build/run_*`, the boundary has been breached.

**Part B — the evidence**: the six-tier ladder with what each tier does *not* license, the three-place declaration rule, the four requirements, the rule that every check must be shown to fail, what the frame oracle licenses, per-item acceptance criteria for the seven remaining subsystems, and the anti-patterns.

The row I'd point at is **the Vulkan backend: reachable tier `none`, explicitly unverifiable, correctness inherited from the software backend it mirrors, and it must say so.** A subsystem with no reachable tier is allowed — it just can't borrow credibility from the checks around it.

**Claude**

Confirmed: `0x000001BA` pack headers — the three intro movies are plain **MPEG-1 Program Streams**, video plus audio. So yes, you're right, and I've been stating the rule too loosely. Let me fix the statement.

## The distinction I've been eliding

**"Dependency-free" is a property of the verification path, not of the program.** Everything `verify.py` touches — the format readers, the runtime, the reference backends, all 40 `dump_*`/`run_*` tools — must build with nothing installed. That's what makes 190 checks runnable on a bare checkout, and it's the requirement worth defending.

**The playable frontend will need dependencies and should have them.** Hand-rolling Cocoa + Win32 + X11 to avoid SDL, or writing an MPEG decoder to avoid vendoring one, would be strictly worse: more code, no verification benefit, and none of it a port of anything in the original binary.

## The realistic list

| need | what | why |
|---|---|---|
| window, input, audio device | **SDL3** (system, optional) | one library for all three; the alternative is three platform backends |
| render | **Vulkan loader + MoltenVK** (system, optional) | as decided |
| the three intro movies | **pl_mpeg**, vendored | they're MPEG-1 PS — exactly what it handles. One public-domain file, no build config. ffmpeg is orders of magnitude larger and brings licensing questions for one codec |

Two things that shrink this more than you'd expect:

- **Shaders can be pre-compiled to SPIR-V and checked in.** A fixed-function-era renderer needs a textured vertex-coloured triangle and a blit, so the Vulkan backend needs the *loader* but not glslang or shaderc in the build. That removes the most irritating build dependency.
- **No audio codec is needed.** OTNS ADPCM is already ported and sample-exact against `adp.py` across 777 files. Only a *device* is missing, which is SDL.

And the movies are only a playability dependency — the boot path already steps past them without decoding, which is why `engine: boot` passes today with nothing installed.

## The rule I'd add to `PORTING` A8

Three clauses, and the third is the one that isn't obvious:

1. `make` with nothing installed builds every `dump_*`/`run_*` and passes the suite. A dependency that breaks this is rejected, not worked around.
2. No ported source may include a dependency header. They appear only in backend files, behind the A2 boundary.
3. **No dependency may perform work the reference implementation is supposed to be a port of.** Using SDL's blitter instead of the ported `Blt`, or a library's BMP loader instead of `surfaceFromBmp`, would mean the check tests the library rather than the port — and it would have passed just as green this afternoon while establishing nothing.

Clause 3 is the real content. The first two are hygiene; that one is what stops a dependency quietly eating the evidence.

Also worth splitting **vendored** (small, single-file, checked in, `make` still works — pl_mpeg) from **system/optional** (large, versioned, platform-managed — SDL, Vulkan), because they fail differently: a missing vendored file is a broken checkout, a missing system one should just disable the frontend.

Want me to amend A8 with that before continuing? It's a small edit and it's cheap to do now, while the frontend is still hypothetical and nothing has been built against a wrong assumption.

## The finding that reshaped the task

`sub_4822F0` (line), `sub_4806C0` (triangle) and `sub_480BD0` (quad) each open with `if (sub_45EF50() == 2)` and choose between **Direct3D and the engine's own software rasterizer**. The selector is a display-driver *index*: `sub_43A6D0` gives a real DirectDraw GUID mode 0, and the last two synthetic entries in the device list modes 1 and 2. Mode 2 is the software back end — so there was a rasterizer to *port*, not one to invent.

Two more from reading it:

- **A mode-2 triangle is a wireframe** — three calls to the line rasterizer, no fill. So porting `sub_48C4C0` gave me line *and* triangle.
- **The software path takes its colour from a different place than the D3D one**: `I2D_DrawLine` stores the colour argument at payload dword 6, but `sub_48C4C0` is handed the table lookups of dword **2** — the third component of the first point. Recorded, not reconciled.

The three 565 tables are built by `sub_440A20` from the surface's own channel **masks**, so the conversion follows the pixel format rather than assuming one — 565 is the instance, consistent with the blit already matching by truncation.

## Tier 6, not 4 — stated in the header

The blits reach tier 4 because a `Blt` is a memory copy the captures can be diffed against. These can't: the captures were taken in whatever mode CrossOver picked, which isn't mode 2. A capture with the last driver index would raise the whole row to 4, and that's now in `PORTING` B6 as a concrete next step.

What is asserted — 698,689 pixels over 3000 lines: **0 outside the clip rect**, all four reject arms, **400/400** wireframes exactly the union of their edges, and the reversal test *split in two* — **1541/1541 unclipped** (what the pre-Bresenham swap buys) against **1255/1459 clipped**, because the clip runs before the swap and is asymmetric by construction. The first version reported one number, 2561/3000, and couldn't distinguish a faithful asymmetry from a bug.

## A claim I had to withdraw mid-way

I wrote that the reversal test "catches an error-term slip". It doesn't — initialising the Bresenham error to 0 instead of `-dx>>1` shifts a line half a pixel *symmetrically*, so it still reverses identically, and the mutation moved only 1255→1266. So I added the test that does catch it: **every plotted pixel must be the nearest one to the ideal line**, `|2·(dy·Δx − dx·Δy)| ≤ max(|dx|,|dy|)` in doubled integers. 408,801 probed, 0 off — and the zero-init mutation takes it to **264,696**.

## Left

The quad's mode-2 path is a separate float-based routine (~189 lines) and isn't ported; the 3D view submits a scene and belongs to the render port, not the 2D layer. Both are named in the coverage table rather than implied by silence — and the `porting standard` check caught the B6 table growing from 7 rows to 8, which is what it's for.

**Claude**
